The widths of the confidence intervals (CIs) reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. Essentially, the further you look ahead, the more room there is for unexpected dynamics to play a role.

Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated intervals if they are particularly extreme or occur suddenly. For example, an economic shock, significant policy announcement, or unforeseen crisis could disrupt short-term stability in ways that aren't fully captured by historical data or current assumptions. Similarly, any highly volatile or speculative elements linked to the forecasted variable could create tail risks that lead to outcomes far beyond the forecasted range. While the 90% confidence intervals aim to cover the most likely outcomes, rare and highly impactful events—sometimes called "black swans"—are inherently hard to predict, which would explain why outcomes occasionally fall outside the given intervals.
